doc.title: Oliver Nelson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 10, 2020

chapter: Sound Pieces and Los Angeles studios
title: Does music need meaning? Sound Pieces and Bob Thiele
summary: Beauty over programmatic meaning, and Bob Thiele giving his father license for instrumentations like Flute Salad.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Okay. Now I think I lost my question. Actually this is something I think about a lot. What does music mean? And when he called it “Sound Pieces” he could have called it something descriptive, he could have dedicated it to something. But he called it “Sound Pieces,” just like Samuel Barber called that beautiful piece “Adagio for Strings.”
So I’m struggling to ask my question, but does music have to have a deeper meaning other than it’s just beautiful music?

I think it does not. I think it can just be beautiful. If you read the liner notes on that album you see when he said, “Why did you name that ‘Sound—.’” He said, “It’s a piece that sounds.” That’s what Dad quoted, and I think that’s what he was thinking just beautiful sound and stuff. We would — this is really interesting — but we would get together sometimes and he and I would cry just about beautiful sounds that we would hear and beautiful pieces that we would hear, and that kind of stuff. So beauty to him musically was a big deal. Now some things had special meaning, if you look at “The Kennedy Dream.” And I was thinking about “The Kennedy Dream.” All those pieces have a certain meaning. I mean they were all written for a certain thing. But that “Sound Pieces” was just a creative idea and that’s why I think he loved Bob Thiele so much. Because Bob would give him creative license to do pretty much anything he wanted. And Dad was lucky that he could get people to play instrumentations. “Flute Salad.” You’ve got four alto flutes. I mean especially back then. Now you can find them today but back then who’s got four alto flutes? And then he got a big band with French horns. You hire more people to come in and do this stuff. But Bob loved him enough and knew what he could
do that he would give him license to be able to write pretty much whatever he wants to, which is a really neat thing.
